content: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that affects approximately 50 million people globally, as reported by the World Health Organization in 2015. It is characterized by recurrent, involuntary brain activity that manifests as seizures. This condition is often associated with various comorbidities, including psychological challenges and cognitive difficulties. Cognitive impairment is a significant concern for individuals with epilepsy. A survey involving over 1,000 epilepsy patients revealed that cognitive impairment was their primary concern. Among these cognitive issues, memory difficulties are the most frequently reported, with 20% to 50% of individuals with epilepsy experiencing memory impairments. These memory problems have been shown to have a profound negative impact on quality of life. Several factors can influence memory in people with epilepsy. The use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), seizure foci, interictal epileptiform activity (specific electrical abnormalities in the brain between seizures), and seizure activity itself can disrupt the encoding of new information into memory and the retrieval of previously stored information. Cognitive impairments in epilepsy are often addressed indirectly through effective seizure control, careful selection and adjustment of AED dosages, restructuring of antiepileptic drug polytherapy regimens, and treatment of comorbid depression. However, this systematic review focuses on non-pharmacological interventions aimed directly at treating memory problems associated with epilepsy. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is a device, similar to a pacemaker, that delivers regular electrical stimulation to the brain via the vagus nerve. It is an FDA-approved add-on therapy for reducing seizure frequency in medically refractory partial epilepsy. Clinical evidence supports the efficacy of VNS in reducing and preventing medically refractory seizures, with seizure frequency reductions ranging from 24.5% to 30.9%. However, the effects of VNS on cognition are less well-established. Some studies report memory enhancement, while others describe no change or even deterioration in memory. A small randomized clinical trial found that administering VNS following learning improved word-recognition memory in people with epilepsy. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is another device that generates regular stimulation to specific brain regions via implanted electrodes. It is FDA-approved for treating Parkinson’s disease, dystonia, and essential tremor. Research has demonstrated the efficacy of DBS in reducing seizure frequency in epilepsy. Studies of DBS targeting the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) have reported a 50% or greater reduction in mean seizure frequency in 16% to 100% of epilepsy patients. A multicenter randomized trial of bilateral ANT stimulation in refractory partial epilepsy found that stimulated patients experienced a 40% reduction in seizure frequency compared to 14% in controls. Recent studies have also examined the effects of DBS on cognition in epilepsy patients. One study found that bilateral ANT stimulation was associated with significantly improved performance in verbal fluency and delayed verbal memory tasks. Stimulation of the entorhinal region during learning significantly enhanced performance on a spatial learning task requiring navigation through a virtual environment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive procedure that uses electromagnetic induction to deliver a magnetic field across the scalp, stimulating nerve cells in specific brain regions. Repetitive TMS (rTMS) has been extensively studied as a treatment for various psychiatric and neurological conditions, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, post-traumatic stress disorder, Parkinson’s disease, dystonia, and epilepsy. Several small studies and case reports have demonstrated the efficacy of rTMS in reducing seizure frequency in refractory partial epilepsy and epilepsia partialis continua. Currently, seven randomized controlled trials have examined the efficacy of TMS for seizure reduction in epilepsy, with four studies reporting significant results and three reporting insignificant results. One clinical trial and one case report of rTMS in refractory epilepsy patients with cortical malformations found improvements in some aspects of cognitive functioning. The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, moderate-protein, low-carbohydrate diet used primarily in children for the treatment of refractory epilepsy. It is based on a 3:1 or 4:1 fat-to-protein and carbohydrate ratio, mimicking the biochemical effects of fasting. This diet induces a ketogenic state in the body, leading to a reduction in seizure frequency. Systematic reviews of the ketogenic diet report that approximately 16% of children achieve seizure freedom, and 33% to 56% experience a greater than 50% reduction in seizure frequency. A randomized controlled trial found that the ketogenic diet significantly reduced seizure frequency in children, with 38% of those on the diet experiencing a greater than 50% reduction in seizures compared to 6% in the control group. A recent Cochrane review identified shortto medium-term benefits of the ketogenic diet but noted low tolerability over longer periods. Cognitive rehabilitation is a neuropsychological treatment program focused on training attention and memory functions in individuals with cognitive deficits due to brain injury. These programs primarily aim to compensate for, rather than restore, cognitive deficits. Compensatory strategies can be external, such as using an electronic agenda to store information and remind oneself of tasks, or internal, such as elaborating and visualizing information to facilitate later retrieval. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation programs in treating epilepsy-related memory problems. However, methodologies and program characteristics vary significantly across studies. A randomized controlled trial comparing two cognitive rehabilitation programs—the retraining method and the compensation method—found both strategies to be effective in improving self-reported cognitive outcomes and quality of life in people with epilepsy. The mechanisms of action of VNS and DBS in improving memory are not fully understood. VNS is thought to activate upstream neural networks from the vagus nerve input into the medulla and deep brain structures. Functional imaging evidence suggests that the thalamus and mesial temporal lobe, structures involved in memory, are activated during VNS in patients with epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression. Secondary benefits may occur through improved alertness and attentional capacities, as well as the potential for AED reduction. DBS mechanisms likely depend on the brain region selected for stimulation and the neural network interrelationships with the stimulation targets. DBS therapy in epilepsy has most frequently targeted the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, which is implicated in seizure propagation through cortico-thalamic, mammillo-thalamic, and Papez circuits. DBS may exert a positive, indirect effect on cognition by decreasing abnormal epileptic activity within these pathways. In summary, cognitive impairments, particularly memory problems, are common in people with epilepsy and significantly impact their quality of life. While few therapies exist for directly treating memory problems in epilepsy, non-pharmacological interventions such as VNS, DBS, rTMS, the ketogenic diet, and cognitive rehabilitation show promise. Further research is needed to better understand their mechanisms of action and optimize their efficacy in addressing memory impairments in epilepsy.
